explanations.explanation: Right there in the verse: "He gathers the exiles of Israel." Exiles are people living far from home, and the LORD is the One bringing them in. I know a little about that feeling. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, waiting to be gathered up. Both things happen in the same verse, the city built up and the people gathered.

No courtroom in this verse, friend. The psalm says nothing about judging the exiles. What it says is, "He gathers the exiles of Israel." These are people far from home, and the LORD is the One who brings them together.

This one points the opposite way. The psalm says, "He gathers the exiles of Israel." Gathering means bringing people in, not sending them farther out. It's like a cookie box: everything goes IN, nothing goes flying out the sides.

That's the heart of this whole psalm, friend: "He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds." Healing is what the verse says He does. I think a verse that tender is worth reading twice. Some of you may need that one today.

The psalm doesn't say testing here. It says, "He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds." When someone is brokenhearted, this verse shows the LORD stepping in to heal. I think that's worth slowing down for.

Teaching is a good thing, and I do plenty of it around here. But that's not what this verse says. It says, "He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds." For the brokenhearted, the LORD heals.

explanations.answer: He calls each one by name
explanations.explanation: The psalm says it: "He determines the number of the stars; He calls them each by name." So He settles the number AND He knows each name. I get a little dizzy thinking about it, because my own sky only has six shapes in it. Every one of those shapes has a name I never forget. Think about a sky with every star named.

explanations.answer: He lights each one at dusk
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a nice picture, but the psalm doesn't say it. What it says is, "He calls them each by name." So after He determines the number, the next thing is names. Every star gets one.

explanations.answer: He moves each one by hand
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but this psalm doesn't say that about the stars. It says, "He determines the number of the stars; He calls them each by name." The detail the psalm gives is the names. Each star is called by name.

True. The psalm says, "His understanding has no limit." No limit at all, not even a little one at the edge. I can't even keep track of my own mixing bowls, so this one is hard for me to picture. That's why the writer calls Him great.
The psalm actually says, "His understanding has no limit." So it's true, not false. Not a single limit anywhere. That's one of the reasons the writer calls our Lord great and mighty in power.

Yes, friend. "The LORD sustains the humble, but casts the wicked to the ground." The psalm puts two kinds of people side by side, and the humble are the ones He sustains. I can tell you from experience, I was pretty humble in the back of that drawer. Nothing humbles a stamper like a dead battery being the most popular guy in the room.

Mighty sounds like it could fit, but the psalm doesn't say it. It says, "The LORD sustains the humble, but casts the wicked to the ground." So the word in the blank is humble. The other side of the verse is the wicked.
Clever is a fine thing to be. But the verse doesn't say it. It says, "The LORD sustains the humble, but casts the wicked to the ground." Humble is the word that goes in that blank.

That's it: "Sing to the LORD with thanksgiving." This is a song with a thank-you inside it. I've got a LOT to be thankful for, like a gold base, a warm oven and an angel who found me. So this one comes easy to me.
The psalm doesn't give trembling here. It says, "Sing to the LORD with thanksgiving." Thanksgiving is the extra thing this second call to praise adds. A thank-you goes right inside the song.
No weeping in this verse, friend. The psalm says, "Sing to the LORD with thanksgiving." The singing comes with thanks. It also says to make music on the harp to our God.

Yep. God "makes grass to grow on the hills." Clouds cover the sky, rain gets prepared for the earth, and then the hills turn green. I just noticed that this is a whole chain from sky to ground. No part of it skips a step.
Thorns would be a prickly surprise, but that's not in this verse. The psalm says God "makes grass to grow on the hills." Grass is the word for that blank. The clouds and the rain lead right to it.
Weeds don't show up in this verse. The psalm says God "makes grass to grow on the hills." The blank is grass. It's a gentler picture than weeds, I think.

Right! He provides food "for the young ravens when they call." These little ones call out, and the psalm says God provides for them. Jesus points to ravens too, saying they neither sow nor reap, and God feeds them (Luke 12:24). I think that's a pretty good picture of being looked after.

Lions are impressive, but they're not the ones in this verse. The psalm says God provides food "for the animals, and for the young ravens when they call." So the little callers are ravens. I bet they're loud about it, too.
Lambs are cute, but they're not in this verse. The psalm says God provides food "for the animals, and for the young ravens when they call." The ones who call are young ravens.

This one is false, friend. The psalm says, "He does not delight in the strength of the horse." A horse is strong, and the verse says that isn't what God delights in. The next line says He takes no pleasure in the legs of a man.

False is right. The psalm says, "He does not delight in the strength of the horse; He takes no pleasure in the legs of a man." Strength is on the list of things He doesn't delight in. I think that takes a little pressure off, because I will never win a race.

That's the one: "The LORD is pleased with those who fear Him, who hope in His loving devotion." The verse before it listed the horse's strength and a man's legs. Here the psalm turns to the people He is pleased with. They hope in His loving devotion.

Giving is a good thing, but it's not what this verse says. The psalm says, "The LORD is pleased with those who fear Him, who hope in His loving devotion." Nothing about who has the biggest pile. It's about those who fear Him and hope in Him.

I love learning, but this verse isn't about who knows the most. It says, "The LORD is pleased with those who fear Him, who hope in His loving devotion." The ones He's pleased with are the ones who fear Him. They hope in His loving devotion.

Yes, friend! "He strengthens the bars of your gates." This is the first reason the psalm gives for Jerusalem to praise. A strong gate bar is the kind of thing nobody thinks about until they need it. The psalm says God is the One who strengthens it.

The temple is a big deal, but it's not in this verse. The psalm says, "He strengthens the bars of your gates." So the thing getting stronger is the bars on the gates. Good to know someone is looking after the small parts.
Towers sound impressive, but the verse doesn't mention a palace. It says, "He strengthens the bars of your gates." That's what God makes stronger in the city.

That's right: "and blesses the children within you." Behind those strong gates, the children are the ones named. I think a verse like that is a happy one. The gate bars are strong, and the little ones inside are blessed.
Priests are important, but they're not named in this verse. The psalm says God "blesses the children within you." The children are the ones inside the gates who are blessed.
No kings in this verse, friend. The psalm says God "blesses the children within you." The ones blessed behind those strong gates are the children. I think that's a sweet detail.

Yes! "He makes peace at your borders." The borders are the edges of the land, and the verse says God makes peace there. And the same verse goes on to say He fills Jerusalem with the finest wheat. I'd say that's a good day at the bakery.
That would be a rough border, but it's not what the verse says. The psalm says, "He makes peace at your borders." Peace is the word for that blank. War doesn't show up in this verse at all.
Walls are a reasonable guess, since the last verse was about gates. But this one says, "He makes peace at your borders." So the blank is peace. It's God who makes it.

True. The psalm says, "His word runs swiftly." God sends forth His command to the earth, and it goes out at speed. Nobody has to chase it down. I can barely get a text back from anybody, so this is impressive to me.
The psalm actually says, "His word runs swiftly." So it's true, not false. He sends forth His command to the earth, and the word is quick about it.

Right! "He casts forth His hail like pebbles." The psalm gave us snow like wool and frost like ashes, and now hail like pebbles. Wool, ashes, pebbles, all in a row. Winter shows up in this psalm with a whole set of pictures.

Rain was in an earlier verse, where God prepares it for the earth (verse 8). But this verse says, "He casts forth His hail like pebbles." The blank is hail. It comes right after the snow and the frost.
Dew is soft, and this verse is not. The psalm says, "He casts forth His hail like pebbles." The blank is hail. It's part of a cold list that also has snow and frost.

Yes. "He sends forth His word and melts them." The snow, frost and hail are all there, and then His word goes out and melts them. The verse goes on to say that when He unleashes His winds, the waters flow. I think that's a pretty good picture of what His word can do.
Hardening would make a colder verse, but that's not what it says. The psalm says, "He sends forth His word and melts them." So after the cold comes the melting. Then the waters flow.
That would be a LOT of snow, but the verse goes the other way. It says, "He sends forth His word and melts them." The cold doesn't pile up. It melts when His word goes out, and then the waters flow.

That's it: "He declares His word to Jacob, His statutes and judgments to Israel." Jacob and Israel are both names the psalm uses here for the people. Jacob is one of Israel's forefathers. God declared His word to them.

Those are real nations in the Bible, but they're not named in this verse. The psalm says, "He declares His word to Jacob, His statutes and judgments to Israel." So the answer is Jacob and Israel. They are the ones He declares it to.
Edom and Moab were neighbors of Israel, but this verse doesn't name them. The psalm says, "He declares His word to Jacob, His statutes and judgments to Israel." The answer is Jacob and Israel.

This one is false, friend. The psalm says, "He has done this for no other nation; they do not know His judgments." God declared His word to Jacob and His statutes and judgments to Israel. The psalm says He has not done this for any other nation.

False is right. The psalm says, "He has done this for no other nation; they do not know His judgments." That's what the verse says about the nations. And then the psalm ends the way it began, with "Hallelujah!"
